source.title: BLUEFIN: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Financial Spreadsheets

output.summary: BLUEFIN is a benchmark for LLM agents working on professional-finance spreadsheet workbooks. It has 131 tasks in three families: synthesis (build a workbook from a prompt), manipulation (modify a given workbook) and interrogation (answer a question about a workbook). Synthesis and manipulation tasks are graded against 3,225 binary rubric criteria in six categories, validated by experts, and scored by an agentic LLM judge (GPT-5.4) whose agreement with experts is high (Krippendorff's alpha 0.826, macro-F1 0.839). Interrogation tasks have a known answer instead. Five frontier models run in an open-source 20-tool harness all score below 50% overall on the held-out set. Their weakest areas are computed output values and dynamic behavior under input changes (perturbation), while static formula correctness is much stronger. The paper also reports cost-performance tradeoffs, model behavior profiles, a small human utility study and case studies. This matters because spreadsheet errors are costly and widely used, yet realistic, hard-to-verify finance tasks have been underserved by benchmarks.
main_claims: Existing spreadsheet and finance benchmarks are shallow, programmatically verifiable or flat-table based, so a benchmark of realistic, multi-step professional finance workbook tasks was needed.

BLUEFIN covers synthesis, manipulation and interrogation tasks and grades them with expert-vetted, granular binary rubrics across six categories (Formula Correctness, Model Integration, Output Validation, Perturbation, Presentation, Pitfalls).

An agentic LLM judge that inspects the workbook with tools and performs perturbation tests reaches expert-level agreement (alpha 0.826, macro-F1 0.839), making rubric grading of hard-to-verify tasks feasible.

Frontier models score below 50% overall on the held-out set, with the best at 49.6% (GPT-5.5) and Opus 4.7 at 49.2%; they do much better on static formula correctness (50-68%) than on Output Validation (20-48%) and Perturbation (15-37%).

Higher cost does not buy better results: GPT-5.5 gets a similar score to Opus at about 5.6x lower cost, and models differ in behavior, such as GPT-5.5's reliance on execute_python and weaker models' rare use of recalculation.
background: What a spreadsheet workbook is: tabs, cells, formulas versus hardcoded values, and cell references
Basic corporate finance models: DCF, WACC, debt schedules, balance sheet, merger/LBO models
Benchmarks and held-out versus public test sets

sections.label: motivation-gap
sections.title: Why a finance spreadsheet benchmark
key_points: Finance is spreadsheet-heavy, and spreadsheet errors have caused large losses, so evaluating AI here matters.
Obstacles: confidential enterprise spreadsheets are hard to obtain, and success includes usability criteria that are not programmatically verifiable.
Prior benchmarks focus on formula generation, atomic edits, flat tables or fixed-spreadsheet QA; related work such as GDPVal, FinSheet-Bench and BankerToolBench differs in scope or task depth.
Spreadsheets differ from code through 2D spatial reasoning, formatting concerns and financial modeling conventions.

sections.label: task-families
sections.title: The three task families
key_points: Synthesis builds a workbook from a prompt (example: a DCF model), manipulation edits an existing workbook (example: adding a debt schedule), and interrogation answers a question about a workbook.
Synthesis and manipulation are scored against rubrics with criteria such as formula correctness, output validation and perturbation; interrogation is auto-graded against a reference answer.
The benchmark has 10 synthesis, 82 manipulation and 39 interrogation tasks, with 3,225 rubric criteria; manipulation tasks need at least 45 minutes of analyst work.
Only 305 rubric criteria over 11 tasks are released publicly; the rest are held out against leakage.

sections.label: dataset-construction
sections.title: How tasks and rubrics were built
key_points: Vetted, well-paid expert contributors made tasks from seed workbooks, writing prompts as they would brief a capable analyst.
Candidate rubric criteria were generated by Claude Opus 4.6 and then validated and refined by human reviewers.
Interrogation tasks were chosen by tracing multi-step calculation chains and have a specified correct answer rather than a rubric.
The held-out manipulation set (n=75) spans five task categories and 16 industries; annotation took about 5 hours per task.

sections.label: rubric-categories
sections.title: The six rubric categories
key_points: Formula Correctness checks the intended calculation; Model Integration checks values link to their source tab instead of being recomputed or hardcoded.
Output Validation checks key outputs within a tolerance; Perturbation changes an input and checks the dependent output recomputes correctly.
Presentation checks formatting conventions; Pitfalls are penalty criteria for errors such as #REF! or truncated text.
Every criterion is binary with a fixed point weight, and no separate structural completeness section was kept because it over-rewarded copying a template.

sections.label: harness-and-judge
sections.title: Evaluation harness and agentic judge
key_points: The agent harness has 20 tools, including a LibreOffice recalculation tool and a sandboxed execute_python, with a deliberately minimal 61-word prompt.
The LLM judge (GPT-5.4, high reasoning) inspects workbooks with the same tools, runs perturbation tests by changing inputs and recalculating, and returns a binary verdict with evidence.
Scores are the weighted ratio of points met to maximum points; interrogation answers are graded component by component against the reference.
The judge was validated on 384 binary criteria (alpha 0.826; macro-F1 0.839 versus 0.803 for Gemini and 0.805 for Sonnet).
The authors acknowledge that richer scaffolding might raise scores.

sections.label: overall-results
sections.title: Overall model performance
key_points: On 120 held-out tasks, GPT-5.5 scores 49.6, Opus 4.7 49.2, Gemini 45.9, Sonnet 42.9 and Grok 31.3; none exceeds 50%.
Synthesis scores are highest, which the authors speculate reflects the freedom of building from scratch versus the brittle constraints of an existing workbook.
Manipulation is the most common task type and models integrate poorly into existing workbooks.

sections.label: failure-modes
sections.title: Where models fail
key_points: Pass rates are highest for Formula Correctness (50-68%) and much lower for Output Validation (20-48%) and Perturbation (15-37%), a gap of roughly 30 points.
Perturbation failures come from hardcoded intermediate values, formulas overwritten by constants, and circular structures that do not converge.
Output Validation errors include sign errors, date misalignment, rate-versus-amount confusion (5.0 instead of 0.05) and wrong discounting timing.
Pitfalls is a penalty section; Grok's high pass rate reflects producing less content.
Across the 75 manipulation tasks the median task score is 46.2%, only 44% of tasks reach 50%, and none reaches 70%.

sections.label: cost-and-behavior
sections.title: Cost tradeoffs and behavior profiles
key_points: The Pareto frontier runs Grok 4.20, Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT-5.5; Opus is dominated, with GPT-5.5 scoring similarly at $8.85 versus $49.21 per task.
GPT-5.5 starts with execute_python on 64% of manipulation tasks, which lowers its turn count but coincides with weaker Output Validation.
Sonnet returned the unchanged input workbook on about 8% of manipulation tasks.
Models that rarely call recalc_workbook (Sonnet, Grok under 50%) have weaker Perturbation pass rates, since they cannot self-verify.

sections.label: case-studies-utility
sections.title: Case studies, human utility study and limitations
key_points: Case 1: a merger-model task where all models scored at most 35%, failing through workbook integration errors and conceptual logic errors such as a partly circular revolver formula.
Case 2: an OpEx tab task where off-by-one row references to the Inputs tab separate Gemini (32%), Opus (64%) and GPT-5.5 (88%).
Case 3: a balance sheet task where Gemini scored 100% at $3.00 and Opus 95% at $83.05, a 27.7x cost ratio, showing average scores can hide cost-per-correct-output differences.
A small utility study with two former finance professionals found Opus most often judged a usable starting point and formatting a consistent weakness across models.
Limitations: each task has one workbook as context and no other artifacts, and a uniform harness may disadvantage models trained for particular harnesses.
